content:
Reduced mobility with arthritis is common, but it is often improvable. Pain, stiffness, weak muscles and fear of falling all play a part, and each can be worked on. A physiotherapist can build an exercise plan. The right walking aid and home changes can make getting around safer. If your mobility drops suddenly, see your GP, as this may need checking.

Why mobility drops

  • Pain in the knees, hips, feet or back makes walking uncomfortable, so you walk less.
  • Stiffness limits how far joints bend, making stairs and getting out of chairs hard.
  • Muscle weakness develops quickly when you are less active and adds to joint strain.
  • Fatigue, common in inflammatory arthritis, saps stamina.
  • Fear of falling can lead people to restrict activity, which weakens balance further.
  • Weight puts extra load on hips and knees.

Related reading: Mobility scooters, arthritis and frailty (UK)

When to get checked

See your GP if your mobility has dropped noticeably over weeks or months, or if you have new swelling, weakness or numbness. Seek help the same day if it changes over days, for example if you suddenly cannot walk, cannot bear weight after a fall, or have new leg weakness. Treatable causes include a flare of inflammatory arthritis, an infection, a fracture or a nerve problem.

Exercise is the foundation

NICE recommends exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis, tailored to the person. For mobility, focus on:

  • leg strength: sit to stand, step-ups on the bottom stair, seated knee extensions
  • balance: standing on one leg holding the worktop, heel-to-toe walking along a corridor
  • flexibility: gentle daily stretches for hips, knees and ankles
  • walking: short, regular walks, building time gradually

You can often self-refer to NHS physiotherapy. Water-based exercise and tai chi are other good options.

Walking aids

The right aid, correctly fitted, can reduce pain and improve confidence.

  • a walking stick held in the hand opposite the painful leg
  • a rollator with a seat for longer distances
  • a wheelchair or scooter for outings where walking is not practical. Your local wheelchair service assesses for NHS chairs.

A physiotherapist can check the height and show you how to use an aid on stairs and kerbs.

Making home easier

  • stair rails on both sides, grab rails and a second banister
  • raising chairs, beds and toilet seats to reduce bending
  • removing trip hazards and improving lighting
  • moving essentials downstairs if stairs are hard

Ask your council for a free needs assessment. An occupational therapist can advise on equipment and adaptations.

Financial and practical help

  • Blue Badge: for people who find walking very difficult
  • Personal Independence Payment (PIP) if you are of working age, or Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age. In Scotland, Adult Disability Payment has replaced PIP.
  • Motability: if you receive the enhanced mobility rate, you can use it towards a car, scooter or powered wheelchair
  • Concessionary bus passes for disabled people in many areas

Look at the bigger picture

Review your pain relief with your GP or pharmacist so that you can exercise. Ask whether any medicines could be making you dizzy or drowsy. If arthritis in one joint is severe despite treatment, your GP can discuss a referral to consider surgery such as joint replacement.

Keeping some movement every day, even when it is limited, protects the mobility you have and helps rebuild what you have lost.

Setting realistic goals

Think about what you most want to be able to do again, such as walking to the corner shop, managing the stairs or getting in and out of the car. Share this with your physiotherapist so your plan targets it directly. Progress is often slow at first, so measure it over weeks rather than days. A simple record, such as how many times you can stand from a chair in 30 seconds, shows change you might otherwise miss.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
